title: Lasem's Plurality
content:
The arrival of migrant groups, especially in Lasem-Rembang, such as the Arab, Chinese, and European communities who admired Javanese culture, even trying to emulate its style so that in their development they became Javanese. This can be considered as the beginning of the cultural crossing process or assimilation between Islam and Ancient Javanese, Chinese, and even strong European cultures at that time (Ricklefs, 2005). Today, Lasem is known and designated as a “Heritage City” considering that in this largest sub-district city in Rembang Regency, many historical sites and relics are found (Wirya, 2018). Therefore, Lasem District is known as a spatial space that bears silent witness to cross-generational cultural blends. Looking at the social plurality in Lasem where Arab, Chinese, Dutch (European), and Javanese communities interact and exchange cultures, this results in a mixed culture and marks a cultural crossing process. The results of the cultural crossing process in Lasem include:

  • Marriages between the Javanese and Chinese ethnicities in Lasem which formed the Chinese-Javanese or Sino-Javanese descent.
  • Material culture or architecture such as; Sunan Bonang's Pasujudan (Prostration Stone), Nyai Ageng Malokah's Tomb, Baiturrahman Grand Mosque, Islamic Boarding Schools, Chinatown residential areas, Chinese Houses, Gie Yong Bio Temple, Cu An Kiong Temple, Regol Port and Dasun Shipyard, as well as Chinese Cemeteries.
  • Tiga Negeri (Three Lands) Batik.
  • Language and Dialect.
  • Culinary.

title: Hybrid Identity: Language
content:
One of the most prominent results of cultural crossing in Lasem is the inclusion of Hokkien (Fújiàn) and Cantonese language elements into the people's daily language. The Chinese community in Lasem, who have settled since the 14th century, brought their language with them, which then mixed with Javanese. For example, many words originating from Chinese have become part of the local vocabulary, especially in the context of trade, culinary, and daily life. Some examples of loan words such as “hauce” (meaning delicious), “goceng” (five thousand), “ceban” (ten thousand) are still used today.

In addition, in daily language, especially among the Chinese descent community in Lasem, a unique mixture of Hokkien dialects and Javanese language structures can be heard. Thus, producing a kind of linguistic creole that adds to the richness of language variations in Lasem.

The known dialects of the Lasem people are as follows:
  1. em/-nem= mu (your in Indonesian). Nggonem/Nggonanem= Yours; (the letter “e” in the word em is pronounced like the “e” in the word perahu (boat) or selasa (Tuesday)) (Nurhajarini, et al., 2015).
  2. leh = toh (Indonesian emphasis particle). Example: Piye leh iki? = How is this? Sampeyan ape ning ndi leh? = Where are you going? (the letter “e” in the word ape is pronounced like the “e” in the word tempe or cafe)
  3. ugung/gung (jw: durung) = belum (not yet in Indonesian). Example: Aku ugung mangan/Aku gung mangan = I haven't eaten yet, and many more (Nurhajarini et al., 2015).

The cultural crossing process in Lasem produces a language rich in mixtures. In the market or in homes, people will speak in a mixture of Javanese with the insertion of Chinese, Arab, or even Dutch words. This phenomenon does not only occur among the Chinese descent community, but also among the local Javanese residents. This linguistic assimilation process shows how language in Lasem develops through mixture and adaptation.

title: Hybrid Identity: Clothing/Batik
content:
The arrival of Europeans as rulers who formed imperialism and colonialism on the island of Java resulted in a meeting process of two cultures, namely Western (European) and Eastern (Asian-Archipelago) cultures. These two cultures are each supported by different ethnicities and have different social structures which then assimilate or acculturate to produce new cultures and identities (Soekiman, 2011).

Likewise in Lasem, when Dutch domination did not necessarily make Lasem residents anti-colonialists. They concocted a traditional cloth, Tiga Negeri (Three Lands) Batik, whose colors reflect the harmony of those three ethnicities. The red color depicts Chinese culture. If the brown color (soga) depicts Javanese culture, then the blue color depicts European culture.

In 1870, batik production had a quite significant development as a contribution of Chinese merchants, and at the turn of the century, the hand-drawn and stamped batik business was experiencing its golden age (Elliot, 2013). According to Kwan Hwie Liong, the daughter of Bi Nang Un is said to be the pioneer in making batik cloth in Lasem (Wei & others, 2016).

Batik in Lasem has its own characteristics by presenting colors from the three ethnicities who settled there. The bright red color known as “abang getih pitik” or chicken blood red is inspired by the red color in Chinese tradition (Perdana, 2012). This color symbolizes luck and prosperity, depicting Chinese culture.

Furthermore, the brown color (sogan) was adapted from Javanese culture. Javanese batik generally has geometric patterns and natural motifs such as plants, leaves, and birds. In Lasem batik, these motifs are not lost, but combined with Chinese elements. Examples of frequently used Javanese motifs are sekar jagad, mega mendung, or the kawung motif, which contains the philosophy of harmony and order in life.

The blue color (indigo) found in Lasem batik depicts the Dutch. Lasem batik motifs have their own distinct characteristics, some originate from native Lasem residents, while others originate from the acculturation of Chinese culture. Tan (1981) asserts that typical Chinese motifs can be seen in the images of the Hong bird, Qilin, Liong (dragon), goldfish, and jungle fowl. In addition, there are also other batik motifs such as latohan, which is a small round motif; watu pecah, shaped like crushed gravel inspired by construction during the Dutch colonial period; gunung ringgit, which is a mountain image inspired by the gunungan in wayang (shadow puppets).

The uniqueness of Lasem batik lies not only in the motifs but also in the use of colors and production techniques. Lasem is known as one of the batik centers with a unique natural dyeing technique, especially in the use of red and blue colors. Red is produced from natural dyes derived from noni roots, while blue is obtained from indigo leaves (Ishwara et al., 2011). The combination of these two colors, along with other colors, produces a soft yet strong gradation, showing the skills of Lasem batik artisans in creating high-quality batik.

title: Hybrid Identity: Culinary
content:
Culinary culture was also impacted by the arrival of the Chinese and Dutch communities. One of the most famous results of this cultural crossing is the Lontong dish (Astuti et al., 2019). Lontong Tuyuhan has become a culinary icon of Lasem. It is said that this culinary delight was the food of the Yellow War fighters.

Then besides food, there is a signature Lasem drink called Kawista Syrup. This beverage is a typical souvenir of Lasem-Rembang. This syrup is made from processed wood apple (kawista) fruit which is processed with water and sugar. Therefore, the taste of this kawista syrup is sweet like cola, so locals usually call this drink the 'Cola van Java' (Bakhtiar & Haryanto, 2018). The results of the cultural crossing in Lasem are not only seen in the ingredients and flavors, but also in the way of cooking, making, and serving food and drinks. Many Chinese cooking techniques, such as steaming, stir-frying, and roasting, were adapted into Lasem culinary arts.

title: Hybrid Identity: Material Culture
content:
Lasem is known as a region rich in historical values and cultural harmony, especially between Islam and the Chinese. The traces of Islam are very strong through various material cultural heritages, such as Sunan Bonang's Pasujudan (Prostration Stone), which was once used as a place for spiritual contemplation by Sunan Bonang in spreading Islam. The Tomb of Nyai Ageng Malokah, an important female figure who was also the Regent of Lasem, helped strengthen the traces of the spread of Islam in this region. In addition, the Baiturrahman Grand Mosque, built in 1588, played a central role in the resistance movement against the VOC in the Yellow War of 1741, and became a strong symbol of Lasem Islam along with the tomb complexes of Kyai Baidhlawi and Mbah Sambu.

On the other hand, Chinese influence in Lasem culture is still clearly visible through the Chinatown settlement in Karangturi. The Chinese houses there feature distinctive architecture such as 'kupu tarung' (butterfly) doors, high windows, altar tables, as well as Ngang Shan model roofs with swallow tail and lotus ornaments that symbolize prosperity. Historical temples such as Gie Yong Bio and Cu An Kiong are not only religious centers but also memorial monuments of the 1740–1743 Yellow War, commemorating the alliance of struggle between the Javanese and Chinese ethnicities represented by figures such as Panji Margana, Oei Ing Kyat, and Tan Kie Wie.

Lasem also holds a maritime heritage through Regol Port and Dasun Shipyard, which have been active since the Majapahit era. Local expertise in shipbuilding is evidenced by the discovery of the Punjulharjo Ancient Boat from the 7th century. Furthermore, the Tomb of Tan Sin Ko, one of the leaders of the Chinese alliance in the Yellow War, has become a symbol of respect for the services of Chinese figures in the anti-colonial struggle. All these remnants prove that Lasem is not only a meeting point of various cultures, but also a place where values of tolerance, resistance, and spirituality grow side by side, strongly recorded in various forms of material culture that are still well-maintained today.
